area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a stall at high power and low speed behaves the way it does, fly a departure stall straight ahead or in a climbing turn within commercial tolerances (heading within 10 degrees, bank no more than 20 degrees plus or minus 10), recover at the point the examiner asks for, and climb away at VX or VY without a secondary stall or a spin.
why: Departure stalls happen low, nose high and at full power, the worst place to lose control: many stall/spin accidents have happened on takeoff, climbout and especially go-arounds [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. High power at low speed also makes the strongest left yaw the airplane can produce, and a stall with yaw is how spins start [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

prereading.label: AFH 5-18 to 5-19
prereading.what: Full stalls, power-on: entry, right rudder, recovery and return to the flightpath. Also the secondary stall.

prereading.label: AFH 5-12 to 5-17
prereading.what: Impending and full stalls, recognition by sight, sound and feel, AOA indicators, stall characteristics and the fundamentals of recovery.

prereading.label: AFH 5-20 to 5-24
prereading.what: Cross-control and elevator trim stalls, the common errors list, spin awareness and the four phases of a spin.

prereading.label: PHAK 5-30 to 5-33
prereading.what: The four left-turning tendencies: torque reaction, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession and P-factor.

prereading.label: AC 61-67C, par 100 to 109
prereading.what: What changes the stall, distractions, stall recognition, power-on (departure) stalls, recovery and the primary cause of spins.

prereading.label: AFH 3-19 to 3-20
prereading.what: Climbs and climbing turns: slipstream pitch-up, P-factor and torque in the climb, and climb errors.

prereading.label: AWH 22-11 to 22-14
prereading.what: Wind shear on takeoff: why a microburst just after lift-off is so dangerous and how little time you get.

warmup: Think first: in a power-off stall the airplane mushes and the nose drops gently. In a power-on stall you are at full power, the nose is far above the horizon and you are holding a lot of right rudder. What do you think happens if your right foot relaxes at the moment the wing stalls?

key_terms.def: A stall practiced at takeoff or climb power and configuration, to simulate a stall during takeoff, climbout or a go-around [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]].
The AOA where airflow separates from the wing and it stalls. It is about 16 to 20 degrees, depending on design, and the same at any airspeed, weight or load factor [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The AOA has caused a stall warning but has not yet reached the critical AOA [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
The critical AOA is exceeded; typically an uncommanded nose-down pitch you cannot readily stop, perhaps with a roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
At high AOA the descending blade on the right takes a bigger bite than the rising blade, so thrust shifts right and the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The corkscrew of air behind the propeller. At high power and low speed it is compact and pushes hard on the left side of the fin [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
The engine turns the propeller one way, so the airplane tries to roll the other way: to the left with a clockwise propeller [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
A force on the spinning propeller acts 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation, so pitch changes cause yaw and yaw causes pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
A stall that follows a recovery, caused by rushing the recovery before the airplane has regained enough flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
The part of a spin from the stall and the start of rotation until the spin is fully developed, often two or more turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
A stall when full power is added with nose-up trim set, as in a go-around, and the nose rises sharply and turns left [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Knowing the margin between your current AOA and the critical AOA; an AOA indicator shows it directly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

chunks.title: The departure stall at commercial standards

body.p: Power-on stalls are practiced from straight climbs and climbing turns of 15 to 20 degrees of bank. They teach you to recognize an accidental stall during takeoff, a go-around, a climb, or an attempt to clear an obstacle [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The typical real-world version: the nose is pitched too high right after takeoff, in a climbing turn, or while trying to clear an obstacle [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

The FAA ties these accidents to a few repeat causes: losing positive control because of a nose-high trim setting, premature flap retraction, and the short-field takeoff [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. Keep those three in mind; they come back in every chunk of this lesson.
The private and commercial ACS share every knowledge and risk element for this Task. The skills differ in who decides how far you go:

head: Element
Private (PA.VII.C)
Commercial (CA.VII.C)
rows: Power (S4)
Set power (as assigned by the evaluator) to no less than 65 percent
Set power to no less than 65 percent
Heading and bank (S6)
Hold them while inducing the stall
Hold them until an impending or full stall is reached, as specified by the evaluator
Cues (S7)
Acknowledge cues of the impending stall, then recover promptly after a full stall occurs
Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall
Recovery (S8)
Recover in accordance with the POH/FM
Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall, as specified by the evaluator
SRM (S11)
Listed as its own element
Not listed in this Task

body.p: Table source: ACS PA.VII.C.S4 to S11 and ACS CA.VII.C.S4 to S8. Tolerances are the same at both levels: a specified heading within 10 degrees straight ahead, or a specified bank no more than 20 degrees, plus or minus 10, in a turn (ACS CA.VII.C.S6).

callout.text: So at the commercial level you must be ready for either recovery point. If the examiner asks for an impending stall, letting it go to a full stall is unsatisfactory, as is an excessively low pitch attitude or excess airspeed, altitude loss or a spin in the recovery [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].
The POH/AFM procedure and power setting for your airplane come first. Always follow the manufacturer's recommended stall procedures when they are published and current [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: The examiner says 'power-on stall, climbing turn to the right, recover at the first indication.' What does 'first indication' mean for you?
check.a: Recover at the first stall cue, such as the horn or buffet, without letting it reach a full stall (ACS CA.VII.C.S7, S8). A full stall here would be unsatisfactory [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

body.p: A stall is exceeding the critical AOA, not a lack of airspeed. It can happen at any airspeed, any attitude and any power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. Power changes everything around that AOA: the attitude, the speed, the yaw and the cues.

bullets: Attitude: at climb power the airplane can hold a much higher nose before it stalls. That is why the AFH has you slow to lift-off speed before adding power: to avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude for a long time before the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

Speed: a propeller's slipstream adds lift over the wing behind it. The AFH points out what jets lack: no slipstream to lower the power-on stall speed, and no instant lift from a burst of power [[24:330|AFH 16-21]]. So in your airplane the power-on stall usually comes at a lower indicated speed than the power-off stall. The airspeed indicator arcs mark power-off stall speeds [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]], so at full power the stall may come below the speed you expect.
Cues: in a power-off stall the buffet and shaking are less noticeable than in a power-on stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. At power, expect a louder, rougher stall.
Yaw: torque, slipstream and P-factor make a strong left yaw at high power and low speed. The closer to the stall, the more right rudder you need [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: Weight and balance change how easily you get there. More weight needs a higher AOA for the same lift, so the stall speed goes up [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]]. An aft CG takes less elevator to stall at a given load factor, which makes inadvertent stalls easier and recovery harder; at an extreme aft CG a spin may go flat, and recovery from a flat spin is often impossible [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]. A forward CG stalls at a higher speed and needs more back pressure [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

Load factor: a stall from straight-and-level flight or from an unaccelerated straight climb adds no load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The moment you pull abruptly or tighten a turn, you are in an accelerated stall at a higher speed. Pulling too fast during a power-on stall entry is a listed common error for exactly this reason [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Same wing, same critical AOA. Power only moves where you meet it: higher nose, lower speed, rougher buffet, more left yaw.

Some light-sport airplanes reach a very high nose-up attitude in power-on stalls unless slowed first, and some manufacturers limit the pitch to 30 degrees. Aggressive pitch plus uncoordinated rudder can make a spin entry quick and aggressive [[24:347|AFH 17-13]].

check.q: Why does the AFH have you slow to lift-off speed before you add power for a power-on stall?
check.a: To avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time before the airplane stalls [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

chunks.title: Left-turning tendencies at high power and low speed

body.p: To the pilot, 'torque' is really four separate effects: torque reaction, the corkscrew of the slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. The airplane's builder offsets them for cruise, where it spends most of its time, so at climb power and low speed you must make up the difference yourself [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

head: Effect
What it does
When it is strongest
rows: Torque reaction
Rolls the airplane left, opposite the clockwise propeller [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
High power
Spiraling slipstream
Strikes the left side of the fin and yaws the nose left; also makes a small rolling moment to the right [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
High propeller speed and low forward speed, as in takeoffs and power-on stalls [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Gyroscopic precession
A pitch change makes a yaw, and a yaw makes a pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
Abrupt pitch changes; best known when the tail is raised on a tailwheel takeoff roll [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
P-factor
Moves the center of thrust to the right, so the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
High AOA, which means nose high and slow [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]

body.p: In a climb the AFH puts it plainly: torque and P-factor roll and yaw the airplane to the left, and you counter with right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. In the power-on stall entry, as the speed bleeds off, you move the elevator further back and add right rudder at the same time, all the way to the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

The effects also change during the recovery. As you lower the nose and the speed builds, P-factor and the slipstream force fade, so the right rudder you were holding becomes too much. Application of the PHAK rule that any pitch change makes a yaw: a quick pitch-down acts like raising the tail, which the PHAK says yaws a clockwise-propeller airplane to the left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Expect the rudder demand to change quickly, and fly the ball, not a fixed foot position.

callout.text: The ball tells you which foot. If the ball moves right as the nose yaws left, you need more right rudder. Re-center it continuously; the AFH lists not keeping coordination with rudder through the stall and recovery as a common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

These forces vary greatly between airplanes, engines and propellers, and from one phase of flight to the next. It is the pilot's job to correct for whichever one is strongest at the time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

check.q: Which two left-turning tendencies grow most as the nose rises and the airspeed falls toward a power-on stall?
check.a: P-factor, which grows with AOA, and the spiraling slipstream, which is most compact and strongest at high power and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

chunks.title: Coordination, yaw and the road to a spin

body.p: A spin needs two things: at least one wing past the critical AOA, and sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall. Yaw comes from wrong rudder, but also from adverse yaw, engine and propeller effects, and wind shear [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. A departure stall has all the ingredients built in: high pitch, high power and low airspeed. The AC calls this a classic setting for P-factor to play a role in a stall/spin accident, during a go-around or short-field takeoff [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

bullets: The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA while using too much or too little rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

In uncoordinated flight the pitot-static instruments, especially the airspeed indicator and altimeter, become unreliable, so you may not know the critical AOA is near until the stall warning sounds [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].
A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can spin the airplane in the direction of the rudder, whichever wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
In a turning stall, a slip may let the outer wing stall first and drop abruptly; a skid may let the bank steepen to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: Watch the ailerons too. Training wings stall root first so the ailerons keep some effect, but if a wing drops and you use aileron to lift it before lowering the nose, the down aileron raises that tip's AOA and can deepen its stall and roll you further into it [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Reduce the AOA first, then roll level.

How fast it goes: an incipient spin lasts about 4 to 6 seconds and about 2 turns in a light airplane, per the figure. The first turn loses about 1,000 feet and each later turn about half that [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. A departure stall near the ground leaves no room for any of it.

callout.text: Single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics must not have a tendency to inadvertently depart controlled flight [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. That protects you only in coordinated, normal handling. Modern airplanes are reluctant to spin, but mishandled controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can still spin them [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Stall plus yaw equals spin. Keep the ball centered so the stall has no yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: In a power-on climbing turn to the left, you let the nose yaw left with too little right rudder and the airplane stalls. Which way is it likely to spin, and why?
check.a: To the left. The yaw (here a skid to the left from P-factor and slipstream) sets the direction; a stall in a skidding or slipping turn spins in the direction of the yaw and rudder, whichever wing is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

chunks.title: Knowing it is coming: cues and warning systems

body.p: You learn to recognize an impending stall by sight, sound and feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. In a departure stall each cue looks a little different:

bullets: Feel: control pressures get lighter, you need bigger control movements, and the airplane responds more slowly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Just before the stall, buffeting, uncontrollable pitching or vibration may start [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

Sound: the noise of the air along the airframe drops as you slow [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. With a fixed-pitch propeller you may also hear and see an RPM loss approaching a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].
Vision: the airplane can stall in any attitude, so the picture out the windshield is not a foolproof cue, though pitch awareness still matters [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Kinesthesia: the seat-of-the-pants sense of changes in speed or direction warns a trained pilot in visual flight [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

body.p: Stall warning devices: certification requires a clear and distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. It can come from the airplane's own pre-stall buffet or from a device such as a horn, light or stick shaker; many vintage, light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device at all [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Many devices warn 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

An AOA indicator shows your stall margin directly, but it has limits: calibration, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]]. Some indicators account for flap position and some do not [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

head: Warning limitation
What it means on departure
rows: The published 1G stall speed is valid only unaccelerated, coordinated, at one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
A climbing turn, a gust or a heavy aft load moves the stall to a different speed
A stall warning system may fail [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Use the other cues: buffet, loss of roll authority, or inability to stop a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Ice, frost or contamination [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]]
The stall may come with little or none of the usual cues, at a speed well above normal [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]]
Noise in the flight deck
Application: high power is loud; the horn is easier to miss in a climb than in a glide

callout.text: Even a small amount of snow, ice or frost on the wing raises the stall speed; flight should not be attempted with it on the surfaces [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]].

check.q: Your airplane has no AOA indicator and the stall horn is inoperative. Name two cues that still warn you of a power-on stall.
check.a: Any two of: lighter controls and slower response, buffeting or vibration, the change in air noise, an RPM loss with a fixed-pitch propeller, and seat-of-the-pants feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

body.p: On departure, a stall warning is never 'just the horn'. Every normal departure has moments where you are slow, nose high and at high power. The sources point to these:

bullets: Short-field takeoff: rotating early or climbing too steeply can make the airplane settle back or hit obstacles, and below VX the climb stays flat [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
Climbing at VX: in some airplanes a 5-knot error from the recommended speed costs a lot of climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. There is little margin either way.
Go-around: the trim is set for low speed, so full power raises the nose and yaws it left. Letting the nose rise too early can mean an unrecoverable stall at low altitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Flap retraction: raising the flaps all at once can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; premature flap retraction is a known factor in departure stall accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]].
Gusts: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA, and the airplane may stall while you fight to control the flightpath [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

body.p: The AFH's energy example shows how a normal climb turns into a stall warning: a hot afternoon departure from a high airport, slow acceleration, poor climb, rising terrain, the pilot gradually pitches up, the climb stops, and the stall horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]]. The non-intuitive fix is to give up some altitude to gain speed so the airplane can climb again [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

callout.text: When one or more stall indicators appear, starting the recovery should be instinctive, unless you are practicing a full stall at a safe altitude on purpose [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. On departure, the instinct is to lower the nose, not to pull.
Treat a horn after lift-off as an AOA problem, not a power problem. You are already at full power, so the only control left that fixes it is the elevator [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: Climbing out toward rising terrain on a hot day, your climb stops and the horn sounds. What does the AFH say you must do, even though it feels wrong?
check.a: Trade some altitude for airspeed by lowering the nose, so the airplane reaches a speed where it can climb again [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

chunks.title: Recovering from a stall that is already at full power

body.p: The most important action for an impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA. Pilots who instead put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The power-on stall makes this trap easier, because power is already in.

bullets: Reduce the AOA immediately, with as much nose-down input as it takes to stop the stall warning [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Level the wings with aileron and coordinate with rudder [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Power: since the throttle is already at climb power, this step may just mean confirming the setting [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Return to the desired flightpath, and only then, with enough airspeed and control effectiveness, set the power you want [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: How much forward pressure? Every airplane needs a different amount, from relaxing back pressure to real forward pressure. Too much puts a negative load on the wing and hinders the recovery [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. An abrupt push forward gives a feeling of weightlessness [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. Power helps: on a propeller airplane it adds airflow over the wing and reduces the altitude lost, but it never fixes a stall by itself [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

Impending stall or full stall, the technique is the same; training should emphasize one recovery for both [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. The only difference is when you begin it. For the impending stall you are recovered once you are back on the desired flightpath with enough airspeed, good control and no stall warning [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

callout.text: Two power-on recovery errors from the AFH list: trying to recover with power before reducing the AOA, and trying to level the wings before reducing the AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
As the nose comes down at full power, the yaw changes fast. Keep working the rudder to stop any yaw while you add or confirm power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

check.q: In a power-on stall, why can't 'add power' be your main recovery action?
check.a: Power is already at the climb setting, and power alone does not eliminate a stall. Only reducing the AOA does [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and what the examiner checks)

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the real power setting, flap setting and speeds.

bullets: 1. Pick an altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.C.S2) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. Clear the area, at and below your altitude, and keep clearing while you slow [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
3. Set the configuration the examiner asks for: takeoff, departure or cruise (ACS CA.VII.C.S3). The AFH normally uses takeoff configuration but also wants practice clean [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
4. Slow to normal lift-off speed while holding altitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
5. At lift-off speed, set takeoff power or the recommended climb power, never less than 65 percent (ACS CA.VII.C.S4), and establish the climb attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
6. If a turn is asked for, roll into the specified bank, not more than 20 degrees (ACS CA.VII.C.S6). The AFH uses 15 to 20 degrees [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
7. Smoothly raise the nose to the stall-inducing attitude and hold it: more back elevator and more right rudder as the speed decays, wings at the set bank, ball centered [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
8. Say the cues out loud at the first indication (ACS CA.VII.C.S7). Recover there, or hold it to the full stall if that is what was asked (ACS CA.VII.C.S8).
9. Recover: reduce AOA until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate, confirm power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
10. Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY (ACS CA.VII.C.S9), then return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gives you (ACS CA.VII.C.S10).

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Altitude (S2)
An entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.VII.C.S2)
Configuration and coordination (S3)
Takeoff, departure or cruise configuration as specified, coordinated throughout (ACS CA.VII.C.S3)
Power (S4)
No less than 65 percent power (ACS CA.VII.C.S4)
Heading or bank (S6)

'Maintain a specified heading ±10° if in straight flight; maintain a specified angle of bank not to exceed 20°, ±10° if in turning flight, until an impending or full stall is reached, as specified by the evaluator' (ACS CA.VII.C.S6)
Cues and recovery (S7, S8)
Acknowledge cues at the first indication; recover at the first indication or after a full stall, as specified (ACS CA.VII.C.S7, S8)
After recovery (S9, S10)
Configure as recommended, accelerate to VX or VY, return to the specified altitude, heading and airspeed (ACS CA.VII.C.S9, S10)

body.p: Power: the AFH single-engine text says maximum power for takeoff stall practice, or less in some airplanes to prevent an excessively high pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. In the AFH's multiengine chapter, a passing remark worth knowing: without a recommended setting it uses about 65 percent of maximum available power, and reduced settings can simulate higher weights and density altitudes [[24:268|AFH 13-19]].

callout.text: Leveling off after the climb-out: start about 10 percent of your climb rate before the target altitude, for example 50 ft early at 500 fpm, then hold climb power until you reach cruise speed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

check.q: The examiner specifies a 20 degree bank for a turning power-on stall. What bank range meets the commercial standard?
check.a: 10 to 30 degrees: the specified 20 degrees plus or minus 10 (ACS CA.VII.C.S6).

chunks.title: After the recovery: VX, VY, cleanup and the second stall

body.p: Many power-on stalls go wrong after the stall is broken. A secondary stall comes from rushing the recovery before the airplane has regained enough flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. Near the ground the natural impulse is to bring the nose up quickly and abruptly; not reducing the AOA enough, or trying to break the stall with power only, does the same [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. If it happens, recover again the same way [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

bullets: VX gives the most altitude over a given distance; VY the most altitude per unit of time. Use VX until clear of obstacles, then VY [[24:142|AFH 6-10]] [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
On a short-field climb, keep gear and flaps in takeoff position until clear of obstacles and stable at VY, then raise the flaps in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
Keep your eyes outside until obstacles are cleared instead of reaching for the gear or flap controls [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
Trim: the climb attitude needs nose-up trim to hold without heavy back pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. After a recovery, retrim as you settle the climb so the airplane is not fighting you.

body.p: The elevator trim stall is the go-around version of the departure stall. With nose-up trim for a glide, full power plus propwash over the tail makes the nose rise sharply and turn left. Firm forward pressure and then retrimming prevent it; taken to a full stall it needs a big nose-down attitude and a big altitude loss [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. You will not fly it on the checkride, but you must know how to prevent it [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

The accelerated stall shows up here too: a hard pull to regain the climb attitude raises the load factor and the stall speed. The pull-up after a stall recovery is where significant load factor increases are sometimes induced [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

callout.text: Break the stall, then earn the climb. Speed first, then pitch, then cleanup in steps.

check.q: After a full power-on stall, you lower the nose, then pull back quickly to stop the altitude loss, and the buffet returns. What happened and what do you do?
check.a: A secondary stall from hastening the recovery before regaining flying speed. Reduce the AOA again until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate, and return to the flightpath more gradually [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Density altitude, turbulence and microbursts on departure

body.p: High density altitude reduces engine and propeller performance, lengthens the takeoff roll and cuts climb performance [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. A normally aspirated engine loses power as altitude increases [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. But altitude has little or no effect on the indicated stall speed; the true airspeed is simply higher for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

That combination is the departure trap. The airplane may lift off in ground effect and then be unable to climb out of it under high density altitude, high temperature or maximum weight; climbing out of ground effect needs a higher AOA and more thrust [[24:142|AFH 6-10]] [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Take off at the recommended speed under marginal conditions, and do not pull for a climb the airplane cannot give you [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a significantly higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

Microburst on takeoff: in accidents studied, the takeoff looked normal for about the first 5 seconds after lift-off, yet the airplane crashed off the end of the runway about 20 seconds after lift-off [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. As airspeed fell, the pilots lowered the pitch to regain trim speed and lost altitude [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]. Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to recognize and respond [[28:269|AWH 22-14]]. A microburst can have downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

callout.text: A rapid or large airspeed increase near convective weather may mean an airspeed decrease is coming next [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]], so the real defense is not to take off under one.

check.q: At a hot, high airport, will your airplane's indicated stall speed be higher than at sea level?
check.a: No. Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed; your true airspeed is higher, and your power and climb are lower [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]] [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

body.p: Clear the area of traffic at and below your altitude before any stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Clearing turns are the core of most clearing procedures; their point is to be sure the next maneuver does not enter another aircraft's flightpath [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. During training, say it out loud: 'clear left, right, above and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

A power-on stall points the nose high above the horizon for a long time. Application: that hides the airspace ahead and above, so clear before you raise the nose. In real climbs, the PHAK recommends gentle banks left and right so you can keep scanning [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

Distractions are how real departure stalls start. Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely while the pilot is busy with something else: a checklist, a chart, fuel figures, an item on the floor or the back seat, or a windy traffic pattern [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Instructors are asked to distract you just before a power-on stall and talk about the effect [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200b]], and the ACS tells evaluators to use realistic distractions on the practical test (Commercial ACS, Use of Distractions).

bullets: Task priority on departure: airplane control comes first. Be careful reaching for the flap handle while high control pressures are present [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Surprise and startle can disrupt your thinking and your muscles at the moment of a stall [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Expecting the wing drop and the rudder change ahead of time is your best defense.
Disoriented pilots may not know their error. Many upsets happen while the pilot's attention is on another task, away from the instruments and outside references [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
After recovering, a listed error is losing situational awareness and not returning to the desired flightpath or following ATC instructions [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Brief yourself before every practice stall: altitude for the recovery floor, heading, the cue you will recover at, VX or VY, and the altitude to return to. Then you have a plan to come back to after the stall breaks.

check.q: Why is the power-on stall a worse collision risk than straight-and-level flight, and what is the fix?
check.a: The high nose blocks your view ahead and above while you are slow and climbing. Clear at and below your altitude before you raise the nose, using clearing turns [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Pulling too fast during the entry, causing an accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Smooth, progressive back pressure; let the speed decay (ACS CA.VII.C.S5)
Not enough right rudder; the airplane yaws left in the climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Add right rudder as the speed drops; keep the ball centered [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Climbing with one wing low from fixating on the nose [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Use the wingtips as well as the nose to set the climb attitude [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Not keeping a constant bank in a turning stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Pick the bank before you raise the nose and hold it to the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Recovering before the critical AOA when a full stall was asked for [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Hold the attitude until the full-stall cues appear [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Letting an impending stall become a full stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Recover at the first indication when that is what was asked [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]
Leveling the wings or adding power before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Nose-down input first, until the warning stops [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]
Excessive forward pressure, low or negative G [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Only as much nose-down as it takes to stop the warning [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Secondary stall or excess airspeed in the recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Return to the flightpath smoothly; watch the airspeed build [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Not clearing the area [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Clearing turns and a call-out before every entry [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]

callout.text: Slow first, power second, pitch smoothly, right foot always. At the cue: nose down, wings level, ball centered, climb away.

check.q: Your CFI sees the nose drift left and the wing dip left in the entry every time. What two fixes come first?
check.a: More right rudder as the speed decays, and use the wingtips, not just the nose, to hold the attitude and keep the wings level [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-12. Power-on stall. (AFH 5-18)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a yellow path from left to right: it slows to lift-off speed holding altitude, sets takeoff power and raises the nose, stalls and lowers the nose with the wings level, stops the descent as flying speed returns, climbs at climb airspeed while cleaning up, and returns to the desired flightpath.

f2.caption: Figure 5-48. Corkscrewing slipstream. (PHAK 5-31)
f2.alt: A high-wing airplane seen from above and behind. An orange arrow labeled Slipstream spirals from the propeller around the fuselage and strikes the vertical tail, labeled Force, while a blue arrow at the nose shows the resulting yaw.

f3.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f3.alt: Two side views of an airplane nose. At low angle of attack the arrows for the load on the upward moving and downward moving propeller blades are equal. At high angle of attack the arrow for the downward moving blade is larger than the one for the upward moving blade.

f4.caption: Figure 5-9. A conceptual representation of an AOA indicator. (AFH 5-14)
f4.alt: Three airfoils: A at 10 degrees with smooth airflow, B at 16 degrees with some separation behind the wing, C at 17 degrees with heavy separation. Three matching AOA indicator faces show a blue ring for A, red chevrons for B and a single red chevron for C. A lift coefficient graph rises with angle of attack to a peak near 2.0 at B and drops after it at C.

f5.caption: Figure 5-16. Spin Entry and Recovery. (AFH 5-23)
f5.alt: An airplane stalls and drops into a spiral around a vertical column. A close-up shows the rising wing less stalled, with more lift and less drag, and the descending wing more stalled, at a greater angle of attack with more drag. Boxes describe the incipient spin (about 4 to 6 seconds, about 2 turns), the fully developed spin (about 500 feet per 3-second turn in small trainers) and the recovery (about one quarter to one half turn after antispin inputs).

f6.caption: Figure 22-14. Wind Shear Encounter During Takeoff After Lift-Off. (AWH 22-12)
f6.alt: A jet airliner shown at four numbered points. At 1 it is on the runway. At 2 it has just lifted off and climbs into the curved outflow lines of a microburst. At 3 it is level, then descending. At 4 it strikes the ground beyond the end of the runway.

scenario.title: Heavy, hot and climbing toward a storm
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot hired to reposition a four-seat airplane with two passengers and bags from a 5,500 ft elevation airport on a hot afternoon. The bags put the CG near the aft limit. Tall trees stand off the departure end, and there are building cumulus with virga about 10 miles west. Your POH gives a short-field takeoff procedure with 10 degrees of flaps and a VX climb. A passenger asks you to circle back over town on climbout for photos.

questions.q: How do the elevation, heat and load change this departure?
questions.a: High density altitude cuts engine and propeller performance and climb, and lengthens the takeoff roll [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. A heavier airplane stalls at a higher speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]], and an aft CG needs less elevator to stall, so over-rotation is easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]].

questions.q: The airplane feels ready to fly well below VX. Should you pull it off and climb?
questions.a: No. In these conditions it may lift off in ground effect but be unable to climb out of it; take off at the recommended speed [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Premature lift-off adds drag and gives a flat climb below VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

questions.q: Climbing at VX over the trees, the stall horn chirps in a gust. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat it as a real AOA warning and relax back pressure to regain VX; a gust can raise the AOA suddenly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], and recovery from stall indicators should be instinctive [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. In some airplanes 5 knots off VX costs a lot of climb, so fly it precisely [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

questions.q: Clear of the trees, you want to raise the flaps and start the photo turn. What order and what limits?
questions.a: Establish VY first, then raise the flaps in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Keep the turn shallow: steep banks reduce or kill climb performance [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Fly it coordinated with right rudder for the left-turning tendencies [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

questions.q: While you look for the photo spot, a passenger points out the town and asks a question. The airspeed is drifting down. What is the risk?
questions.a: Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is distracted by other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Keep the airplane first and scan for traffic with gentle banks while climbing [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: Heading west, the airspeed suddenly jumps 15 knots and the climb improves, under the virga. What next?
questions.a: Expect a possible airspeed loss next; a large airspeed increase near convective weather can mean a decrease is coming [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Turn away from the storm; microbursts can have 6,000 fpm downdrafts and 30 to 90 knot headwind losses [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

skills.do: Clear the area at and below your altitude before the maneuver, with clearing turns.
skills.practice: Make two clearing turns and say 'clear left, right, above and below' before every stall [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Choose an entry altitude that lets you finish the Task no lower than 1,500 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before each lesson, write down the highest terrain in the practice area and your minimum entry altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Set the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration the examiner asks for, and stay coordinated the whole time.
skills.practice: Practice in both takeoff and clean configurations, and keep the ball centered with right rudder as the speed drops [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Set no less than 65 percent power.
skills.practice: Find your POH's recommended power for power-on stalls and the throttle setting that gives it; slow to lift-off speed before adding it [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Move smoothly from the takeoff or departure attitude to the attitude that causes the stall.
skills.practice: Raise the nose progressively and hold it; never jerk it, which risks an accelerated stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Hold a specified heading within 10 degrees straight ahead, or a specified bank of no more than 20 degrees, within 10 degrees, in a turn, until the impending or full stall the examiner specified.
skills.practice: Pick a heading reference on the horizon or a bank you can see against the wingtip before raising the nose; practice turning stalls at 15 to 20 degrees [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Say the cues out loud at the first indication of the stall, such as buffet or the stall horn.
skills.practice: Call 'horn', 'buffet' or 'mushy' aloud on every practice stall so the examiner hears your recognition [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

skills.do: Recover at the first indication or after a full stall, whichever the examiner specifies.
skills.practice: Alternate impending and full stalls in each lesson, using the same recovery technique for both [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

skills.do: Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: After each recovery, call the target, VX or VY, and raise flaps in increments once climbing [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner specifies.
skills.practice: Brief the return altitude before entry; lead the level-off by about 10 percent of your climb rate [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

quiz.q: Which commercial ACS power setting applies to the power-on stall?
options: Exactly 75 percent power
Idle power
No less than 65 percent power
No more than 65 percent power
quiz.why: The commercial standard is to set power to no less than 65 percent (ACS CA.VII.C.S4). The AFH single-engine text uses takeoff or recommended climb power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

quiz.q: Which accident causes does AC 61-67C link to power-on (departure) stalls?
options: Nose-high trim, premature flap retraction and short-field takeoffs
Stretching a glide after engine failure
Steep turns above maneuvering speed
Crossed-control base-to-final turns only
quiz.why: The AC names failure to maintain positive control due to nose-high trim or premature flap retraction, and short-field takeoffs [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. Base-to-final and glide stretching are power-off stall scenarios [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: Why is a propeller airplane's power-on stall speed usually lower than its power-off stall speed?
options: Slipstream adds lift over the wing behind the propeller
P-factor adds lift to the right wing
The critical AOA increases with power
The airplane is lighter at high power
quiz.why: The AFH contrasts jets, which have no slipstream to lower the power-on stall speed [[24:330|AFH 16-21]]. The critical AOA does not change [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: Which left-turning tendency is strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in a power-on stall?
options: Weathervaning
Gyroscopic precession
The spiraling slipstream on the fin
Adverse yaw
quiz.why: At high propeller speed and low forward speed the spiral is compact and pushes strongly on the vertical tail [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. Precession needs a pitch or yaw change [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

quiz.q: What two things must be present for a spin?
options: A forward CG plus a skid
Full power plus flaps extended
A stall on at least one wing, plus sideslip or yaw
High airspeed plus a steep bank
quiz.why: A spin occurs when at least one wing exceeds the critical AOA with sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

quiz.q: According to AC 61-67C, many stall warning devices activate about how far before the stall?
options: 4 to 8 knots
Exactly 10 percent above VS1
1 to 2 knots
15 to 20 knots
quiz.why: Many airplanes have stall warning devices that alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

quiz.q: During a departure the horn sounds as the climb stops toward rising terrain. What does the AFH energy example recommend?
options: Pitch up further to clear the terrain
Raise the flaps right away
Lean the mixture fully
Gain speed at the expense of some altitude
quiz.why: The non-intuitive fix is to gain speed by giving up some altitude, so the airplane can climb again [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

quiz.q: In a power-on stall recovery, the throttle is already at climb power. What does the power step become?
options: Raising the flaps
Confirming the proper power setting
Adding carburetor heat
Reducing to idle
quiz.why: Since the throttle is already at climb power, this step may simply mean confirming the setting [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

options: Leveling the wings with rudder
Using full power in the recovery
Holding the nose down too long
Hastening the recovery before regaining enough flying speed
quiz.why: A secondary stall is caused by trying to hasten the completion of a stall recovery before the airplane has regained sufficient flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

quiz.q: What does high density altitude do to the indicated airspeed at which your airplane stalls?
options: Little or nothing
Lowers it
Doubles it above 5,000 ft
Raises it about 2 percent per 1,000 ft
quiz.why: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed; true airspeed is higher for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

final_quiz.q: Checkride: the examiner asks for an impending power-on stall. You hear the horn, hold on a second longer, and the nose drops on its own. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; the commercial ACS always requires a full stall
You let it become a full stall when an impending stall was asked for
You should have reduced power to idle first
You exceeded the 1,500 ft AGL minimum
final_quiz.why: An uncommanded nose-down pitch is a full-stall indication [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The impending stall maneuver is unsatisfactory if a full stall occurs [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]; the commercial ACS has you recover at the point the evaluator specifies (ACS CA.VII.C.S8).

final_quiz.q: You enter a power-on stall from cruise speed by adding full power and pulling straight up. What does the AFH say goes wrong?
options: P-factor disappears
The airplane cannot reach the critical AOA
The stall speed drops to zero
An excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time before the stall
final_quiz.why: Slowing to lift-off speed before advancing the throttle avoids an excessively steep nose-up attitude for a long period before the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: In a right climbing turn at full power you are holding so much right rudder that the ball is out to the left. If the airplane stalls now, which way is a spin most likely?
options: To the right, the direction of the rudder
Straight ahead with no rotation
To the left, because P-factor always wins
To the left, because the left wing is high
final_quiz.why: A stall in a skidding or slipping turn can spin the airplane in the direction of the rudder application, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. In a skid, rotation is in the direction the controls are applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

final_quiz.q: At the stall the left wing drops sharply. You instinctively turn the yoke right. Why is that dangerous?
options: The down aileron on the left wing raises its AOA and can deepen the tip stall
Ailerons do nothing at the stall
It adds too much right rudder
Right aileron causes a secondary stall on the right wing only
final_quiz.why: The down-deflected aileron on the dropping wing increases its AOA and can roll the airplane further left; reduce the AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a limitation of an AOA indicator listed by the AFH?
options: It only works at maximum gross weight
It cannot work below 1,500 ft AGL
Some indicators do not account for flap position
It replaces the need to clear the area
final_quiz.why: Some indicators take flap position into account but not all; other limits include calibration, unheated probes or vanes and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

final_quiz.q: Which configurations does the AFH want power-on stalls practiced in?
options: Clean only, never with flaps
Normally takeoff configuration, and also clean with flaps and gear up
Landing configuration only
Whatever configuration gives the highest pitch attitude
final_quiz.why: Airplanes with flaps or retractable gear should normally be in the takeoff configuration, but power-on stalls should also be practiced clean to cover all takeoff and climb configurations [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The ACS lets the evaluator pick takeoff, departure or cruise (ACS CA.VII.C.S3).

final_quiz.q: Just after lift-off near a thunderstorm, the airspeed falls with your attitude unchanged. Per the AWH studies, what made similar accidents worse?
options: Pilots used too much right rudder
Pilots lowered the pitch to regain trim airspeed and lost altitude
Pilots raised the flaps too slowly
Pilots climbed at VX instead of VY
final_quiz.why: As the airspeed decreased, pitch was reduced to regain trim speed, available performance was not used and the airplane lost altitude [[28:267|AWH 22-12]]. Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available [[28:269|AWH 22-14]].

final_quiz.q: After a power-on stall recovery you push hard and feel light in the seat, and the airspeed builds quickly. Which error is this?
options: Secondary stall
Elevator trim stall
Excessive forward-elevator pressure causing low or negative G
Cross-control stall
final_quiz.why: Excessive forward pressure in recovery causing low or negative G is a listed common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; too much forward pressure puts a negative load on the wing and hinders recovery [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

final_quiz.q: Your rental airplane is approved for spins in the utility category, but today it is loaded in the normal category with bags aft. Why does that matter if a departure stall turns into a spin?
options: It only changes the stall warning margin
Spins are impossible in the normal category
The normal category has a lower VX
It may not be recoverable from a spin that goes beyond one turn or 3 seconds
final_quiz.why: An airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in the normal category may not be recoverable from a spin beyond one turn or 3 seconds, whichever is longer [[13:12|AC 61-67C 108]]. Recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

final_quiz.q: On a go-around from a full-flap approach, you add full power with nose-up trim set. The nose rises sharply and swings left. What prevents a stall?
options: Raise all the flaps at once
Let the nose rise; the airplane will settle at VY
Firm forward pressure and right rudder, then retrim
Reduce power back to idle and land anyway
final_quiz.why: Expect considerable forward pressure and enough right rudder for torque and P-factor, then rough-trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Propwash plus nose-up trim causes the elevator trim stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Why does AC 61-67C warn that airspeed and altitude readings can mislead you near a departure stall in uncoordinated flight?
options: The airspeed indicator only reads true airspeed
The pitot tube freezes at high AOA
Uneven air pressure over the fuselage makes the pitot-static instruments unreliable
The altimeter lags 30 seconds in climbs
final_quiz.why: In an uncoordinated maneuver the pitot-static instruments are unreliable because of uneven air pressure over the fuselage, so the pilot may not know the critical AOA is near [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out with a passenger, you look down to find a dropped chart and the nose creeps up. Which source finding explains why this is so dangerous?
options: Climb attitude stays constant without pilot input
Distractions only matter in instrument conditions
The stall horn always gets louder during distractions
Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is distracted
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C lists retrieving items from the floor, charts and checklists as distractions that lead to stalls from poor airspeed control [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH want precise airspeed during a VX climb after a short-field takeoff?
options: VX is the only speed at which the stall horn works
Below VX the airplane cannot stall
In some airplanes a 5-knot error significantly reduces climb performance
VX is higher than VY in most airplanes
final_quiz.why: In some airplanes a deviation of 5 knots from the recommended speed may significantly reduce climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. VX is usually slightly less than VY [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

takeaways: A power-on stall is the takeoff, climbout and go-around stall: low, nose high and at full power.
Same critical AOA; power only gives you a higher nose, a lower stall speed, a rougher buffet and more left yaw.
Right rudder grows as the speed drops and changes fast in the recovery. Fly the ball; stall plus yaw is a spin.
At the first cue: reduce AOA, level the wings, coordinate, confirm the power. Power alone never breaks a stall.
Commercial checkride: power at least 65 percent, heading within 10 degrees or bank 20 or less within 10, recover where the examiner says.
After the break: earn the climb. VX or VY, flaps up in steps, no abrupt pull, no secondary stall.
Hot, high, heavy, gusty or near storms: the departure stall gets closer, and a jump in airspeed near a storm can mean a loss is next.
cfi_notes: The commercial S7 and S8 let the examiner choose impending or full stall. Train both in the same lesson so the applicant never assumes; the AFH calls a full stall during an impending-stall maneuver unsatisfactory [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].
The ACS is silent on entry airspeed. The AFH gives lift-off speed before power is added [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]; teach that and explain why, since starting faster gives an extreme pitch attitude.

Sources differ on power: the ACS minimum is 65 percent (ACS CA.VII.C.S4); the AFH single-engine text says maximum power, reduced in some airplanes to avoid an excessive pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Brief the POH setting and make sure it is at least 65 percent.

AC 61-67C (2000) says to smoothly apply maximum allowable power after reducing AOA [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. The newer AFH says to add power as needed and stresses that power does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Teach the AFH and the manufacturer's procedure.

Spin numbers differ. The AFH text says the first turn costs about 1,000 ft and later turns about half [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], while its Figure 5-16 and AC 61-67C use about 500 ft per 3-second turn [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. The AFH text says the incipient phase may take two to four turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]; the figure says about 2. Teach them as rough estimates.

The AWH wind shear advice (hold or raise pitch, accept lower airspeed) comes from studies of large airplanes with stick shakers [[28:267|AWH 22-12]] [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. It seems to conflict with 'reduce AOA first' [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The sources do not reconcile the two for light airplanes; teach stall recovery at any stall warning and microburst avoidance as the real defense.
Students often over-learn 'right rudder' and still hold it as the nose comes down and speed builds. Have them fly the ball through the whole recovery, not a fixed foot position.
Add a realistic distraction just before the stall as AC 61-67C 200b suggests [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200b]], and debrief what the distraction did to the entry and recovery.

Gyroscopic yaw from a quick pitch-down in the recovery is the lesson's own application of PHAK 5-32 [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. No source describes how big it is in a nosewheel trainer; present it as one more reason the rudder demand changes fast.
gaps: Airplane-specific power settings, configurations, pitch limits, VX and VY, flap retraction speeds and the manufacturer's stall recovery procedure come from the POH/AFM.
The sources give no way to measure 65 percent power in a particular airplane; use the POH power tables.

Current 14 CFR 23.2150 requires a clear and distinctive stall warning with sufficient margin but gives no knot value [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. The 4 to 8 knot figure is from AC 61-67C (2000) [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; check your POH for your airplane's warning margin.
No source gives power-on stall speeds for a typical trainer or says how much lower they are than power-off speeds; the airspeed indicator arcs show power-off values [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]].
No source gives a light-airplane wind shear escape procedure; the AWH guidance comes from large airplane studies [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].
How fast a particular trainer drops a wing in a power-on stall, and how aggressively it enters an incipient spin, depends on the airplane and its loading. Ask a CFI who knows the type.

activities.title: Which turning tendency is it?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the effect it describes.

items.t: The engine turns the propeller one way, so the airplane tries to roll the other way
On the ground it puts more weight and drag on the left main tire
A corkscrew of air hits the left side of the fin
Weakens as forward speed increases and the spiral stretches out
A force on the propeller acts 90 degrees ahead in the direction of rotation
Best known when the tail is raised on a tailwheel takeoff roll
The descending blade takes a bigger bite at high AOA
Zero when the propeller shaft points straight into the relative wind

activities.title: How a departure stall becomes a spin
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the chain of events in order, then tap Check.
steps: Nose-high climbing turn at high power after takeoff
Airspeed decays and the AOA rises
P-factor and slipstream yaw grow stronger
Right rudder is not increased, so the nose yaws left and the ball moves right
One wing exceeds the critical AOA with yaw present
The more-stalled wing drops and rotation begins: the incipient spin

activities.title: True or false: cues and warnings
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: With a fixed-pitch propeller, an RPM loss may warn of an approaching power-on stall.
cards.why: True. In fixed-pitch propeller airplanes a loss of RPM may be evident approaching a stall in power-on conditions [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

cards.s: Every certificated airplane has a stall warning horn or light.
cards.why: False. Many vintage, light-sport and experimental airplanes have no stall warning device; certification allows the warning to come from pre-stall buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Because the nose is so high, the view out the windshield is a reliable stall cue in a power-on stall.
cards.why: False. The airplane can stall in any attitude, so vision is not a foolproof indicator [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: A stall warning system can fail, so you should cross-check other cues.
cards.why: True. Other cues include aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority or an inability to stop a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

cards.s: With ice on the wing, the stall may come with few or none of the usual cues and at a higher speed.
cards.why: True. Contamination can remove the usual cues, and the AOA at upset may be below the normal stall warning AOA [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]].

cards.s: The buffet is usually gentler in a power-on stall than in a power-off stall.
cards.why: False. The buffeting and shaking are less noticeable in the power-off stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

activities.title: Work the departure stall numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your engine is rated at 160 hp. What is the least power that meets the commercial ACS power-on stall standard?
items.why: 65 percent minimum (ACS CA.VII.C.S4): 160 x 0.65 = 104 hp. Use your POH power table to find the throttle setting that gives it.

items.q: Same idea with a 180 hp engine: what is 65 percent power?
Terrain under the practice area is 1,800 ft MSL. You expect to lose 400 ft in the recovery. What is the lowest entry altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL?
After the recovery you climb at VY at 700 fpm back to the assigned altitude. How many feet before it should you start the level-off?
items.why: Lead by about 10 percent of the climb rate: 700 x 0.10 = 70 ft [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

items.q: A stall with yaw becomes a spin, and the first two turns are completed before recovery starts. Using the AFH text rule, about how much altitude is lost?
items.why: First turn about 1,000 ft, each later turn about half: 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

activities.title: What set up the departure stall?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the hidden factor that pushed the wing toward the critical AOA.

pairs.l: Hot afternoon, high field, climbing toward rising terrain
pairs.r: Less power available, so speed decays as the pilot pitches up

pairs.l: Rotating well before VX on a short field
pairs.r: High drag and a flat climb below VX

pairs.l: Flaps raised all at once at low speed
pairs.r: Sudden loss of lift and settling
Airspeed loss at the same attitude

pairs.l: Bags loaded at the aft CG limit
pairs.r: Less elevator needed to reach a high AOA

pairs.l: Go-around with nose-up trim and full power
pairs.r: Nose rises sharply and turns left

pins.label: Takeoff roll and lift-off look normal

activities.title: Hot and high departure, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a loaded four-seat airplane out of a 6,000 ft elevation airport on a hot afternoon, with rising terrain beyond the runway and build-ups to the west. Your POH calls for 10 degrees of flaps for the takeoff.

steps.s: On the takeoff roll the airplane feels light well before your planned lift-off speed.
options: Pull it off now and climb steeply
Fly at the recommended speed; if it lifts off early, lower the pitch and accelerate in ground effect
Raise the flaps on the roll
Hold it down with firm forward pressure until VY
steps.why: Under high density altitude the airplane may lift off but not climb out of ground effect; take off at the recommended speed [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. If it lifts off early, level off just clear of the runway to accelerate rather than forcing it down [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

steps.s: Climbing out, the terrain rises faster than you climb. You have pitched up a little at a time and the airspeed is 8 knots below VY.
options: Pitch up more to out-climb the terrain
Lower the nose to regain VY even if it costs a little altitude
Pull the power back to cool the engine
Retract the flaps all at once
steps.why: In the AFH's energy example the climb stops and the horn sounds after gradual pitch-up; the fix is to gain speed at the expense of some altitude [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

steps.s: In a shallow left climbing turn toward lower ground, the horn sounds, the nose is yawing left and the ball is out to the right.
options: Hold the attitude and add left aileron
Reduce the AOA until the horn stops, then level the wings with right rudder to center the ball
Add full power and keep the nose up
Push the yoke full forward
steps.why: Reduce the AOA first, then level the wings and coordinate with rudder [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Stall plus yaw can start a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and too much forward pressure gives a negative load [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

steps.s: The horn has stopped and speed is building. Your passenger says 'we're losing altitude!'
options: Pull up hard to stop the descent
Raise the remaining flaps right now
Stop the descent smoothly, establish VY, then raise the flaps in increments
Lower the nose further to gain 30 knots
steps.why: Hastening the recovery causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]; the pull-up is where load factor rises [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. Retract flaps in increments once at VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

steps.s: Now level and heading away from the terrain, the airspeed suddenly jumps 15 knots near the build-ups.
options: Enjoy the free climb and continue west
Treat it as a possible microburst; expect an airspeed loss next and turn away from the storm
Pull the power to idle to keep the speed down
Climb steeply to use the extra energy
steps.why: A rapid or large airspeed increase near convective weather may signal a coming decrease [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to respond [[28:269|AWH 22-14]].
